title: Why does a clock’s second hand seem to stop when you glance at it?
hook: The first second you see on a clock lasts longer than the rest.
summary: As your eyes move to the clock, the brain stretches the image back in time, so the first tick seems longer: this is chronostasis.

cardBlocks.text: Sometimes, when you glance at an analogue clock, the second hand seems to stay still for longer than normal before it moves. This is the stopped-clock illusion, a kind of time illusion called chronostasis: the first impression of something newly in front of us can seem stretched in time.

A study published in the journal Nature in 2001 explained what happens. When you move your eyes to the clock, the brain extends the image of the target backwards in time, to just before your eyes began to move. This happens every time we move our eyes, but we only notice it when there’s a time reference, such as the second hand.
When you glance at a clock, the brain stretches the hand’s image backwards, and the first second seems longer.

deepDiveBlocks.text: According to the authors, this stretching is one of the mechanisms that "fill in" the gap left by saccadic suppression, the brief cut in vision while the eyes jump. If the target is moved unexpectedly during the eye movement, the illusion disappears.
The effect can stretch apparent durations by up to half a second. It also turns up in hearing and touch, not only in vision.
